checkpoints: Running GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS and no COUNT forces Redis to walk every geohash cell touching the full radius before any distance pruning happens, so a 50km circle hands back a candidate set far larger than anything a rider match actually needs.

Capping the radius to a business-appropriate constant and adding a COUNT parameter lets Redis stop early once it has the nearest handful of sorted candidates, shrinking both the geohash cell walk and the size of the downstream candidate list.

Awaiting `redis.exists` inside a for-loop, once per candidate, is a textbook N+1 pattern: each check is its own network round-trip, so end-to-end latency grows linearly with the candidate count even though the EXISTS lookup itself is sub-millisecond work on Redis's side.

Collapsing the per-driver EXISTS calls into a single ioredis pipeline turns many sequential round-trips into exactly one, which matters more for tail latency under load than shrinking the GEO query itself, since the N+1 loop is the dominant cost.

A periodic sweeper — a cron job or a keyspace-notification listener that runs ZREM on drivers whose heartbeat has expired — keeps the GEO key itself mostly clean over time, so the per-query online filter has progressively less stale data left to check.

Reducing round-trips does not by itself prove the optimization is safe: validating it requires asserting the returned driver set is identical before and after the change for a normal-size radius, while separately confirming the round-trip count drops and p99 latency measurably improves.

The exact radius cap and COUNT value are a business tuning decision rather than a fixed technical constant — setting them too small risks under-returning drivers in sparse areas, so the numbers need to be chosen and validated against real matching needs per market.

If the sweeper falls behind on removing expired heartbeats, stale entries can still pass the per-query EXISTS filter, letting the online/offline signal drift out of sync with the GEO key between sweeper runs.
